title: Vitals submission metadata may identify the patient
description: Even if the payload were limited to heart rate and blood pressure values, the submission from a wearable to the remote monitoring platform is likely accompanied by account, device, or session metadata that can reveal which patient is submitting the measurements.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly list identifiers or metadata fields, so this is based on the common need to associate wearable submissions with a specific patient record.

title: Daily vital-sign combinations can link repeated submissions to the same individual
description: A longitudinal stream of daily heart rate and blood pressure measurements can act as a quasi-identifier when combined over time, enabling records in this flow to be linked to the same patient even if direct identifiers are minimized.
uncertainty_note: This threat is strongest if the platform attempts pseudonymization or de-identification; the flow description does not state whether such measures exist.

title: Platform may create attributable logs of patient vital submissions
description: When the remote monitoring platform receives daily vitals, it will commonly log timestamps, source account/device, and submitted values, creating retained evidence that a specific patient submitted health data at a particular time and reducing deniability.
uncertainty_note: Logging is typical for such platforms but not explicitly stated in the provided flow description.

title: Observed transmission patterns may reveal patient monitoring activity
description: An observer who can see network traffic between the wearable/patient side and the remote monitoring platform may detect that the patient is participating in ongoing health monitoring from the existence, timing, or frequency of daily submissions, even if content is protected.
uncertainty_note: The transport protections are not described, so this focuses on detectability from traffic patterns rather than plaintext exposure.

title: Vitals in transit could be disclosed if transmission is not adequately protected
description: The flow carries sensitive health data from the patient to the remote monitoring platform. If transmission security is weak or absent, heart rate and blood pressure data and associated metadata could be exposed to network observers as an implicit side-effect of the data flow.
uncertainty_note: The description does not specify whether encryption in transit is present.

title: Patient may lack clear notice about granularity and purpose of daily vital collection
description: The patient may not be adequately informed about how frequently daily vitals are collected, what detail is transmitted from the wearable, and how the platform will use those measurements beyond immediate monitoring.
uncertainty_note: No notice, consent, or privacy explanation is described for this flow.

title: Platform may not provide sufficient patient access or control over submitted vitals
description: If the remote monitoring platform accepts daily vitals but does not let the patient inspect, obtain, or otherwise intervene in the handling of their submitted health data, the patient lacks meaningful control over their PHI.
uncertainty_note: The flow itself does not mention patient-facing access or correction features; this is a plausible risk derived from the absence of stated controls.

title: Collection and handling of daily vital data may violate minimization or related privacy principles if broader than necessary
description: Daily submission of sensitive health data to the remote monitoring platform can create compliance risk if the platform collects more granularity, metadata, or frequency of measurements than is necessary for the monitoring purpose, or if it handles PHI without appropriate privacy controls.
uncertainty_note: HIPAA § 164.514 is specifically about de-identification rather than a general minimization rule, so the citation is approximate and mainly relevant where re-identification or insufficient de-identification is implicated.

title: Patient records can be linked across submissions via unique identifiers
description: Incoming vitals stored in the EHR database will typically be associated with a persistent patient or device identifier so measurements can be attached to the correct record. This enables linking multiple submissions over time to the same individual.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly name the identifier, but storing vitals in an EHR generally requires some persistent linkage key.

title: Stored vitals are directly identifying when written into identified EHR records
description: Because the destination is an EHR database, incoming vitals are likely stored together with explicit patient identifiers or within a directly identified patient chart, allowing the subject's identity to be directly revealed.
uncertainty_note: The description does not enumerate fields, but EHR records are commonly directly identified.

title: EHR storage creates attributable evidence of submissions
description: Persisting incoming vitals in the EHR database is likely to create a timestamped, attributable record of what data was submitted and when, reducing the ability to deny that the submission or associated patient event occurred.
uncertainty_note: This assumes normal EHR persistence and auditability practices; explicit logging details were not provided.

title: Sensitive vitals in the EHR database may be accessible more broadly than necessary
description: Storing incoming vitals in a centralized EHR database increases exposure of sensitive health data if access controls are broader than functionally necessary or storage is insufficiently protected. This creates a disclosure risk at the datastore.
uncertainty_note: The existence and quality of access controls are not described; this is a risk inherent to storing sensitive health data in the datastore.

title: Data subjects may lack effective control over stored vitals in the EHR
description: Once incoming vitals are stored in the EHR database, data subjects may not have practical means to access, correct, delete, or stop further maintenance of those records through this flow, creating intervenability concerns.
uncertainty_note: No user-control features or patient rights mechanisms are described for this storage flow.

title: EHR storage may violate minimisation or storage-limitation principles if more data is kept than necessary
description: If the platform stores incoming vitals in the EHR database in greater detail or for longer than necessary for care purposes, this flow would create a compliance risk under core data-protection principles governing minimisation and retention.
assumptions: This threat is contingent on the system storing more vitals data, metadata, or retention duration than is necessary.
uncertainty_note: Potentially also implicates GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) for retention, but the flow description alone does not establish actual over-retention, so the citation is approximate to the principle most directly tied to collection/storage scope.

title: Direct patient identification in nurse-to-EHR updates
description: The nurse's direct review and annotation of a patient's vitals in the EHR database likely transmits or references explicit patient identifiers together with clinical data, making the patient's identity directly revealed within this flow.
uncertainty_note: Assumes the EHR update includes or is bound to explicit patient identity, which is typical for direct charting but not explicitly enumerated in the flow text.

title: Irrevocably attributed nurse annotations in the EHR
description: Annotations entered by the nurse into the EHR database are likely stored as authored clinical content with attribution and persistence, creating a record the nurse may be unable to later deny or retract.
uncertainty_note: EHR systems commonly preserve author attribution and amendment history, but the exact immutability or removability of annotations is not stated.

title: Potential over-granular vital-sign annotation
description: Direct nurse annotation into the EHR may include more fine-grained patient details or contextual notes than are strictly necessary for the immediate clinical task, increasing disclosure risk if excessive granularity is captured.
uncertainty_note: This is plausible for free-text annotations, but the flow description does not specify whether only minimum necessary fields are permitted.

title: Broad accessibility of highly sensitive patient data in the EHR datastore
description: Storing reviewed vitals and nurse annotations in the EHR database creates a risk that sensitive patient information is accessible more broadly than necessary if datastore access is wider than the immediate care context requires.
uncertainty_note: The threat depends on actual EHR access controls, which are not described; this identifies exposure risk at the datastore rather than asserting a known control failure.

title: Patient may lack transparency about ongoing annotation and use of vitals data
description: The patient may not be adequately aware that nurses are directly reviewing and annotating their vitals in the EHR during rounds, nor how those annotations may subsequently be used or viewed within care operations.
uncertainty_note: In routine healthcare this processing is often expected, so this is a weaker transparency risk absent facts showing missing notice practices.

title: Potential failure of data-minimization or confidentiality principles for EHR annotations
description: If the EHR stores more detailed annotations than necessary or makes them accessible beyond authorized personnel, the processing could violate core data-protection principles around minimization and confidentiality.
assumptions: This non-compliance risk is derivative of the identified data-disclosure concerns rather than a confirmed legal violation on the stated facts.
uncertainty_note: No directly applicable healthcare privacy section in the provided regulatory context clearly governs this nurse-to-EHR flow; CLIA provisions supplied appear laboratory-specific, so citation is left empty.

title: Weak recipient verification can identify the patient to unintended call recipients
description: Relaying genetic test results by direct phone call may rely on weak verification (e.g., answering the patient's number is treated as sufficient), allowing identity to be inferred or confirmed by whoever answers and tying the sensitive results to the patient.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the physician discloses or confirms identity/results before robustly verifying the callee; the flow description does not specify verification steps.

title: Phone-call observability can reveal that the patient is involved in genetic-result communication
description: A direct call from the attending physician to the patient may be observable through telecom metadata, caller ID, timing, voicemail notifications, or by nearby persons, allowing others to detect that the patient is engaged in a medical interaction concerning test results even without hearing the full content.

title: Verbal transmission of genetic results may implicitly disclose sensitive data to unintended listeners
description: Communicating genetic test results and next steps by phone can implicitly disclose highly sensitive health information to network operators, voicemail systems, household members, coworkers, or others within earshot if the call is overheard, recorded, or answered by someone else.

title: Genetic test results may be exposed to a dynamically determined unintended recipient
description: Because the physician is calling a phone number rather than interacting in person, the actual recipient may vary at the moment of delivery: the patient, a family member, a caregiver, voicemail, or another person who has access to the device. This creates disclosure risk to parties beyond those functionally necessary.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether identity/authorization is verified before disclosure and whether voicemail/messages are left.

title: The patient may be unaware of the disclosure granularity and call-handling risks
description: The patient may not be informed in advance that highly sensitive genetic test results and follow-up instructions will be delivered over a direct phone call, nor of the associated risks such as voicemail, shared devices, or overhearing, limiting meaningful awareness of how detailed information will be disclosed.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether the patient was informed beforehand or consented to phone-based disclosure.

title: Disclosure of genetic results by phone may be unlawful if made to an unauthorized recipient
description: If the physician releases genetic test results during the call to someone other than the patient or an authorized personal representative, the disclosure may lack a valid authorization basis and constitute an impermissible PHI disclosure.
uncertainty_note: CLIA directly governs laboratory report release, while this flow is physician-to-patient communication of results; the citation is relevant by analogy to authorized-recipient requirements, but applicability to the physician's call itself is not explicit in the provided text.

title: Sequencing report likely contains explicit patient identifiers during handoff/upload
description: The courier-delivered sequencing report and uploaded results are likely to include explicit patient identifiers needed to match results to the correct patient, directly revealing identity at the source side of this flow.
assumptions: Assumes the sequencing report contains patient name, medical record number, accession number, or similar identifiers to support traceability.

title: Results store can link genetic results across records via unique patient/report identifiers
description: If the uploaded sequencing results are stored with persistent patient, specimen, accession, or report identifiers, the destination store can link multiple genetic records and related events to the same individual.
assumptions: Assumes DS2 retains persistent identifiers alongside genetic results.

title: Stored uploaded report and metadata may create attributable evidence of submission
description: Retention of the sequencing report, upload timestamps, courier/lab attribution, or audit metadata in the results store can create an attributable record of who submitted what and when, reducing deniability.
assumptions: Assumes DS2 stores upload metadata or audit trails together with the report/result record.

title: Physical delivery and upload activity can reveal that a subject has genetic testing results
description: The act of courier delivery and result upload may itself be observable to third parties or local observers, allowing detection that a particular person's genetic testing workflow is occurring even without full content access.
assumptions: Assumes the delivery or upload has observable timing, routing, or handling characteristics associated with an identifiable subject or test event.

title: Sequencing report may disclose highly sensitive genetic data beyond minimally necessary content
description: A sequencing report can contain highly sensitive genetic findings and related clinical context. If the full report is delivered and uploaded where a narrower result summary would suffice, this flow discloses more sensitive data than functionally necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the receiving store does not strictly require the full report content or all included genetic details for its intended function.

title: Genetic test results may be released to a recipient outside the authorized chain
description: This flow releases a sequencing report from the external courier/lab side into the results store. If DS2 is not an authorized recipient in the laboratory reporting chain, highly sensitive genetic results are disclosed to an unnecessary predetermined party.
uncertainty_note: Applies if DS2 is outside the set of authorized persons permitted to receive the report; the prompt does not explicitly confirm DS2's authorization status.

title: Stored genetic results may be broadly accessible if the results store is insufficiently protected
description: Once uploaded, highly sensitive genetic results in the store may become accessible more broadly than necessary if storage permissions, segregation, or other safeguards are inadequate.

title: Data subject may not be informed that full sequencing results are delivered and uploaded to this store
description: The flow description does not indicate that the patient is informed that their sequencing report and results are physically delivered and uploaded into this specific store, creating a risk of unawareness about collection and storage.
uncertainty_note: Inference only from absent notice in the prompt; actual patient notice practices are not described.

title: Potential data-minimization or storage-safeguard compliance issue for genetic results in the store
description: If DS2 stores full sequencing reports or exposes them more broadly than needed, the flow may violate core data-protection principles such as minimization and safeguarding for highly sensitive genetic information.
uncertainty_note: This compliance risk depends on whether the full report and access scope are actually necessary and adequately safeguarded.

title: Genetic results and associated attributes can act as a quasi-identifier
description: Genetic test results are highly distinctive and, when combined with patient, sample, or clinical context in the store, can enable linking of records belonging to the same individual across datasets or encounters when pulled by the Clinical Decision Support App.

title: Identity may be inferred from result content or metadata
description: Even if the flow is not stated to include direct identifiers, genetic test results and related metadata may reveal or permit inference of the patient's identity, especially because genomic information is inherently identifying in context.

title: Presence of genetic results may be detectable through application responses
description: When the app pulls results to screen for risk flags, differences in system behavior or responses could reveal whether a patient has genetic results on file or particular report states, allowing detection of involvement or record existence.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether CDS responses differ observably based on the presence or absence of stored genetic results; the flow description alone does not confirm such behavior.

title: Genetic results are disclosed to an additional authorized recipient path that may exceed need-to-know
description: The data store releases genetic test results to the Clinical Decision Support App. Because genetic data is highly sensitive, this flow creates a disclosure risk if the app or its operators are not strictly within the authorized chain and minimum necessary scope for decision support.

title: Clinical Decision Support App may receive finer-grained genetic data than needed for risk screening
description: The stated purpose is to screen for risk flags, which may not require full raw or detailed genetic test results. Pulling complete results into the app could disclose more granular genetic information than functionally necessary for the screening task.

title: Secondary CDS processing of genetic results may be insufficiently transparent to the patient
description: Patients may be unaware that their stored genetic test results are pulled into a Clinical Decision Support App for automated risk-flag screening, which is a distinct processing use with potentially significant implications.
uncertainty_note: The description does not state what notice, if any, is provided to patients about CDS use of genetic results.

title: Use of full genetic results for CDS screening may violate data-minimization or purpose-limitation principles
description: If the app ingests more genetic information than necessary, or uses results beyond the patient-expected clinical purpose without appropriate limitation, the flow can create compliance risk tied to minimization and purpose limitation for sensitive PHI/genetic data.
uncertainty_note: HIPAA § 164.514 is primarily a de-identification provision; this citation is used here only as the closest provided regulatory context on identifiability/minimization risk, not as a direct statement of a HIPAA minimum-necessary violation.

title: Alert content or metadata may identify the patient
description: A flagged high-risk alert sent from the Clinical Decision Support App to the Attending Physician is likely to include identity-revealing clinical content or metadata sufficient for the physician to know which patient is involved. If identifiers or strongly identifying context are transmitted in the alert, the patient's identity is exposed on this flow.
uncertainty_note: This is highly plausible for a clinical alert, but the exact fields in the alert payload are not specified.

title: Alert transmission may create attributable evidence
description: Sending a high-risk alert to the Attending Physician commonly creates timestamped delivery or audit records that attribute the alert and related clinical action context to a specific patient and recipient. Such retained evidence can reduce deniability regarding who received or acted on the alert.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly mention logging or audit trails; this threat depends on typical healthcare-system logging behavior.

title: High-risk alert may disclose PHI to a recipient beyond the minimum necessary
description: The alert conveys sensitive clinical risk information to the Attending Physician. If the physician is not the appropriate authorized recipient for this specific patient, or if the alert includes more detail than needed for clinical action, the flow discloses PHI to a predetermined party beyond what is necessary.
uncertainty_note: The attending physician is often an authorized recipient, so the threat is contingent on misrouting or over-sharing in the alert content. CLIA is most directly about laboratory reports; applicability here is approximate if the alert incorporates lab-derived results.

title: Alert may include unnecessarily granular sensitive data
description: To notify the physician of a flagged high-risk condition, the system may transmit detailed underlying clinical findings, test values, or explanatory context when a simpler risk flag or summary would suffice. This increases disclosure of sensitive PHI beyond the functional need of alerting.
uncertainty_note: The actual payload granularity is not specified, so this is based on a common CDS design risk.

title: Patient may be unaware that their data is used to generate and send risk alerts
description: The patient may not be adequately informed that their clinical data will be analyzed by the Clinical Decision Support App to generate a high-risk alert and that the resulting alert will be disclosed to the Attending Physician. This creates a transparency risk regarding secondary analysis and disclosure of PHI within care workflows.
uncertainty_note: This citation is only applicable if the CDS processing or alerting is part of research or subject to informed-consent requirements; for ordinary treatment operations, Common Rule may not apply.

title: Disclosure in the alert may lack an adequate legal or authorized basis if misconfigured
description: If the high-risk alert discloses PHI to a physician who is not properly authorized for the patient's care relationship, or includes unnecessary PHI without documented authorization where required, the flow creates a compliance risk of unlawful processing or disclosure.
uncertainty_note: The physician is likely intended to be an authorized care recipient, so the risk depends on routing/access-control failures. CLIA applicability is approximate unless the alert functions as or contains a lab report/result.

title: Over-detailed alerting may violate data-minimization principles
description: If the CDS app sends more patient data or more detailed risk information than is needed for the attending physician to take action, the flow may violate core data-protection principles such as minimum necessary use/disclosure and related minimization expectations.
uncertainty_note: No exact section label in the provided regulatory context directly states a general minimization rule for this scenario, so no citation is asserted.

title: Vitals history can be linked to a patient through quasi-identifying clinical attributes
description: Recent vitals history read from the EHR database may contain combinations of timestamps, age-related context, encounter context, or persistent patient references that allow records to be linked to the same individual across accesses and datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the vitals history includes patient-associated metadata or consistent record references rather than fully aggregated anonymous values.

title: Recent vitals history may directly identify the patient
description: The EHR database is likely to return vitals history together with explicit patient identifiers or identity-bearing metadata needed to retrieve the correct chart, which can directly reveal the patient's identity to the receiving application.
assumptions: Assumes the CDS app reads patient-specific vitals from the EHR in a typical clinical context where records are keyed by patient identity.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly list fields, so direct identifiers are inferred from common EHR design.

title: Fine-grained recent vitals history may exceed what the CDS function needs
description: Providing full recent vitals history from the EHR to the Clinical Decision Support App may disclose more granular personal health data than is strictly necessary if the CDS function only needs selected measures, summary values, or a shorter time window.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on whether the CDS logic truly requires the full granularity and time range of the vitals history.

title: Sensitive vitals data is exposed to an additional application party
description: The EHR database makes patient vitals accessible to the Clinical Decision Support App, which increases exposure of sensitive health data to another predetermined system component; this is a disclosure risk if that recipient is broader than functionally necessary or not adequately constrained.
uncertainty_note: The CDS app may be functionally necessary, so the threat is about potential overexposure to an additional party rather than inherently improper sharing.

title: Patients may be unaware that their vitals are reused by CDS processing
description: Using recent vitals history from the EHR in a Clinical Decision Support App can constitute secondary or less-visible processing of patient data, and patients may not be adequately informed that their clinical measurements are being reused for automated support functions.
uncertainty_note: This citation is only relevant if the setting involves human-subjects research or comparable consent obligations; for ordinary treatment operations, applicability is uncertain.

title: Overbroad CDS access to vitals history may violate data minimization obligations
description: If the Clinical Decision Support App reads more vitals data, more history, or more patient detail than reasonably necessary for its decision-support purpose, the processing may violate data minimization and purpose-limitation expectations.
